title: The Didache: two ways
hook: an early handbook: there are two ways, of life and of death; pray the Lord's Prayer three times a day

segments.voice: Yesterday, Luke, and your line was before they forget. Whose story did you write down? Today, a book written for the people learning those stories. Day seven hundred fifty-three.

A short book, only a handful of pages, and it isn't in the Bible. It's something more like a church's handbook: what to teach new believers, how to baptize, when to fast, how to pray, what to do with traveling preachers. Its title calls it the teaching of the twelve apostles. It's very practical. If a traveling apostle stays more than a couple of days, or asks for money, the book says, he's a false prophet. Somebody had clearly met that guy. But the book doesn't open with rules. It opens with a choice.

The word is Didache, Greek for teaching, and its first line says there are two ways, one of life and one of death, and a great difference between them. The picture isn't new. Moses says it in Deuteronomy: "I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life." Jeremiah says it too: "Behold, I set before you the way of life, and the way of death." Jews and Christians share the image. Then the Didache describes the way of life, and it sounds like the Sermon on the Mount turned into a checklist for beginners. Love God who made you. Love your neighbor as yourself. Whatever you wouldn't want done to you, don't do to another. Bless those who curse you. Pray for your enemies. Give to everyone who asks. The way of death is the list of what breaks people: lies, greed, cruelty, pride. Later, the handbook turns to prayer. It gives the Lord's Prayer, the one from Matthew's Gospel that begins "Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name," with a short line of praise at the end, and then a plain instruction: pray it three times a day. Not a new prayer. The same one, three times over, so that the day has a shape. The Didache isn't part of the Bible. But it's a window into how some early Christians tried to live: two ways, and a prayer said again and again to stay on one of them.
screen: `THE LORD'S PRAYER, THREE TIMES A DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the first of three. Settle, and breathe. If you pray, say the Lord's Prayer once now, slowly, one line per breath, and let each line land before the next. Then decide when the other two will be today: midday, maybe, and before sleep. If you don't pray, read or recall the prayer's lines slowly as words, and notice which line catches. Either way, set two small reminders for later. The handbook's idea is simple: the same words, three times, give a day its shape. The bell holds the time.
Didache. Greek for teaching. An early Christian handbook that opens with two ways, of life and of death, and asks for the Lord's Prayer three times a day.
Your line: two ways. Today, at one small choice, ask which way leads to life, and take that one. Then keep your two reminders. Day seven hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: Some Christians pray the Lord's Prayer at set times through the day, and churches that pray morning and evening prayer include it in each service; the Didache is read today as an early Christian writing, not as scripture.

notes: Editor pass: manuscript-discovery claim (Constantinople library) cut under the claims rule; 'morning, midday, evening' cut because the Didache says only three times a day; 'older than the Didache' softened.
The index hook's 'a first-century handbook' was softened to 'an early handbook' under the claims rule (no date in the cited text). Confirm.

The Didache is paraphrased throughout (Lightfoot's 1891 translation exists but the exact wording was not verified). Contents: 1:1 two ways; 1:2 love God, neighbor, negative golden rule; 1:3 bless those who curse, pray for enemies; 1:5 give to everyone who asks; ch. 5 the way of death; ch. 8 the Lord's Prayer with doxology, three times a day; ch. 11 a prophet staying more than two days or asking for money is false. Check each.
'Found again in a library in Constantinople' refers to the Jerusalem Codex (Bryennios); no date is given. Confirm.
'Its title calls it the teaching of the twelve apostles': the manuscript's short title. Confirm.
'The Didache isn't part of the Bible': true of the canons of the major churches; a Keeper may wish to note the Ethiopian Orthodox broader canon discussion.
The practice invites saying the Lord's Prayer (Matthew 6:9–13), not a new prayer.
Audit pass: Didache 11:4–6 applies the two-day and no-money tests to a visiting apostle (who is then called a false prophet), not to a prophet; hook and match pair corrected.
